body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p: The very suspicious title of the new farce at this theatre,—the Trial by Jury,—appeared to announce a full and unmerciful tempest of clap-traps; and when people understood that it was the production of Mr. Theodore Hook, all the puns that have set tables in a roar for the last twelve months, seemed gathering together to aid the storm, and to flash dismay upon us unfortunate critics, who are not allowed, on these occasions, to keep within doors. Who would have thought that these appearances were deceitful? that there should have been very few clap-traps in the piece, and still fewer puns? in short, that Mr. Hook should really have become a little considerate, and found out the vicious nonentity of his friend Joe Miller. Yet, it is very true, farce has little or nothing to do with its name: it is an old story of two gentlemen disguising themselves for love of a young lady, and assailing her heart in her father's house under the respective forms of gardener and footman:—the lady is let into the secret, and chases the gardener; but there is an obnoxious person, as usual, is the case, who is the chosen favourite of her father, and of course a great puppy. The two latter are accordingly deceived, in spite of the perspicuity of the old gentleman, who prides himself on his impossibility of being tricked, and who, by way of illustrating his powers of observation, thinks he has discovered in the footman the son of an old friend of his, upon which discovery he sets aside his former choice, and insists upon giving his daughter away to the happy impostor, till a sudden announcement of the success of the Trial by Jury turns his attention towards the desponding gardener, who proves to be the son above-mentioned, just come into possession of an estate, and therefore fully entitled to his mistress's hand. The reader will easily see, that the piece consists entirely of equivoque; and much of it is certainly very pleasant, though not very new. Equivoque, though one of the lowest parts of dramatic composition, is at least a legitimate part of it, which punning is not; and so far as tricks of plot are substituted for tricks of sound, Mr. Hook has unquestionably improved, — still however in a very negative manner: — he has begun to wean himself of one folly, — no small achievement certainly for a young writer well skilled in the vulgar modes of raising a vulgar admiration; but he has a great deal to do before he can arrive at the means of exciting it in better minds: — the present production is not a jot advanced in anything it has to show for real originality, for delicate observation, for that mature and studious ambition of which Mr. Hook should now begin to think, if he intends to think at all.

The company here was never perhaps in so lamentable a condition, notwithstanding the acquisition of Elliston and Liston, who in the characters of the footman and the coxcomb were the support of the piece, and are indeed almost the only male actors fit to be seen in the theatre. A spectator given to fits of absence might easily fancy himself a hundred miles from London, and start up; at a good clatter of applause, in expectation of seeing the barn come about his ears.
